source.title: Can DPO Learn Diverse Human Values? A Theoretical Scaling Law

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and empirically examines a different scaling relationship: DPO generalization as the number of value clusters changes. It does not test the stated pretraining scaling laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The reported DPO results vary value-cluster count K and measure reward margins, loss, accuracy, or test error. That is not a test of power-law loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute, nor of a compute-optimal split. The tabled held-out errors and reported linear-fit R² values are recorded as findings on a different scaling variable, with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper is a theoretical analysis of DPO generalization against the number of value clusters K and samples per cluster Q, plus fine-tuning experiments on 7-8B models. It varies no parameter count, token count or compute. It fits no pretraining-loss power law and no compute-optimal split. It uses 'scaling law' only for its own Θ(log K) sample-complexity bound. It does not cite or engage the Kaplan or Hoffmann laws, so 'discusses' overstates the link. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors derive bounds showing per-value samples must grow logarithmically with the number of distinct values for DPO to generalize. They report empirical checks on Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B and Qwen3-8B.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and trains with DPO while varying the number of value clusters; it does not use the original pretraining-loss scaling measurement or compute-allocation sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported training and test behavior varies with the number of value clusters K and with training mode (last-layer training versus full fine-tuning); the paper also reports results across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: In DPO fine-tuning, test error rises with the number of value clusters K: Mistral-7B 0.000 to 0.056 and Qwen3-8B 0.000 to 0.183 from K=1 to K=8. Linear fits of test error on K give R² of 0.95–0.99. Theory predicts the samples needed per value grow as Θ(log K).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference-learning generalization degrades with value diversity; per-value sample needs scale logarithmically with the number of values.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
record.problems: The paper's empirical experiments vary value-cluster count rather than model size, training tokens, or compute, so they do not directly evidence the claim versions. Its theoretical guarantees rely on the specified cluster and training assumptions, and the paper notes that it studies in-distribution generalization rather than out-of-distribution settings.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-based reward-margin, loss, and accuracy curves across K are described in the text but are not included as additional rows; the tabled test errors and text-reported fit statistics capture the distinct value-diversity result without treating those curves as tests of the listed versions.

untested.parts: All: no variation of parameters, tokens or compute.
All: DPO fine-tuning is studied, but not loss against scale.

record.verdict_notes: The relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the paper never addresses neural scaling laws in parameters, data or compute. The shared phrase 'scaling law' is the only link to the claim. Rows r2–r8 and r10–r11 share the same correct 'none' link, with no fixes needed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes; the paper studies DPO fine-tuning but not that form against scale.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of the stated laws on setup or fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.
